title: The corner of the field (Mishnah Peah)
hook: how much to leave for the poor, and who may gather it

segments.voice: Yesterday, why blessings come first: before you learn what you owe, you thank for it. Your line: thanks before the harvest. Today, the part of the harvest that isn't the farmer's.

The wheat is down across the whole field except one end. There, a strip of grain still stands, gold and untouched, as if the reapers forgot it. They didn't. The farmer's work is done, and he's gone home. Later, people who own no field at all come with their own sickles and cut it themselves. Nobody hands it to them. Nobody picks who gets some. It's theirs by right. The Torah asks for this strip, and the Mishnah gives it a whole tractate. How big? And who takes it?
screen: `ONE END OF THE FIELD STILL STANDING.` → `THEY CUT IT THEMSELVES.` → `HOW BIG? WHO TAKES IT?`

segments.voice: The corner of the field. In Hebrew, peah. The Torah's command, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corner of thy field." Leave it, it says, for the poor and for the stranger. It never says how much. So the Mishnah, in tractate Peah, asks. It admits the Torah set no measure, then sets a floor: no less than one sixtieth. The right amount depends on the size of the field, the number of the poor, and how good the harvest was. A floor, but no ceiling. A big year and a crowd of hungry people should mean a bigger corner. The second question: who gathers it? The Mishnah says the corner is given while the grain still stands, and the poor reap it themselves. The farmer doesn't cut it and hand it out to people he likes. There are exceptions, grapes on high trellises and dates at the top of tall palms, where the owner brings the fruit down and divides it. But the rule is that the corner isn't the farmer's gift. It belongs to the poor, and they come and take what is theirs. Near its close, the tractate turns to the one who takes. In paraphrase: whoever takes without needing to will not leave the world before coming to need others. And whoever truly needs, and holds back from taking, will live to support others from their own. The corner is for those who need it, and the one who takes is asked to be honest about that.
screen: `PEAH: THE TORAH GIVES NO SIZE.` · `NO LESS THAN A SIXTIETH; NO CEILING.` · `THE POOR REAP IT THEMSELVES.` · `TAKE ONLY IF YOU NEED.` · then, large: `THE CORNER.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you'll have plenty of today: food in the fridge, time, money, patience. Picture its corner, the part you could leave standing for someone else, without deciding who will get it, because that's the point of the corner. Then picture it set where someone who needs it can reach it without having to ask.
The corner of the field. Peah: the edge of the harvest left standing for the poor, at least a sixtieth, and reaped by the poor themselves. Today's word.
screen: `THE CORNER OF THE FIELD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the corner. It's theirs by right, not a favor. Go gently.

howItsDone: Jewish law treats the corner of the field as the poor's by right; where farming laws are kept in the land of Israel, some farmers still leave peah, and Jewish teachers draw on these laws when describing giving that protects the dignity of the one who receives.

chat.says: If a farmer leaves grain for the poor, can't he pick who gets it?
options: No. In tractate Peah the poor reap the corner themselves; it's theirs, not his gift.
Yes. The farmer cuts the corner and hands it to the neighbors he thinks deserve it.
Yes, as long as he leaves exactly one sixtieth; who gets it is his call.
chat.meaning: The Mishnah says the corner is given while the grain stands, and the poor reap it themselves; the farmer doesn't choose who gets it.
